title: landing-hero-incident-to-confidence-variants
body:
Objective:
Capture two linked promises in the homepage hero: (1) Redwood makes inference predictable under real production pressure, and (2) when things go wrong we convert incidents into graceful degradations — preserving product UX and developer SLAs.

Why this brief exists:
Current hero tests lean heavily on speed/cost claims. Engineering buyers care about those, but enterprise/platform buyers (and platform engineering teams) convert on operational assurances: incident windows, consistent p99s, automatic fallbacks, and transparent unit economics during degradation. This doc proposes a set of headline + supporting line variants that place failure-resilience and deterministic economics up front.

Primary audiences and conversion events:
- Platform engineering teams evaluating vendor lock-in, SLAs, and rollout/rollback guarantees. (CTA: Request SLA brief / Dedicated demo)
- Product/ML engineering at AI-native startups who prioritize reliability while optimizing cost. (CTA: Try hosted API / Free credits)
- Security/compliance reviewers who need clear behavior under outages and private deployment options. (CTA: Contact sales / Compliance datasheet)

Hypothesis:
Hero messaging that chains a tangible operational promise (e.g., "99th‑percentile guarantees, plus automatic graceful fallback") with a small proof nugget (SLO examples, fallback tier behaviors) will improve enterprise demo requests and time-to-first-trial for platform teams while keeping PLG conversion roughly neutral.

Headline / subhead variants (tone notes included) — unique, test-ready snippets:
1) Headline: "Keep your app live when the model stops behaving."
   Subhead: "Automatic fallback policies, predictable p99 latency, and cost controls that prevent surprise bills."
   Tone: blunt, operator-first, urgency -> trust

2) Headline: "From incidents to graceful degradation — no guessing."
   Subhead: "Route, revert, or quantize automatically with transparent unit economics at every stage."
   Tone: reassuring, technical

3) Headline: "SLOs you can read, falls you can rely on."
   Subhead: "Per-route SLOs, canary rollouts, and built-in model fallbacks keep experiences consistent."
   Tone: precise, productized

4) Headline: "Control latency, control spend — even under load."
   Subhead: "Workload-aware batching, prefix caching, and tiered model fallbacks reduce cost without surprising users."
   Tone: economic + technical

5) Headline: "Predictable inference. Predictable business outcomes."
   Subhead: "Transparent metrics, SLA-backed capacity, and automatic fallback policies so product teams can ship confidently."
   Tone: executive + operational

6) Headline: "Fallbacks that preserve UX — not just logs."
   Subhead: "Behavior-preserving model variants and routing policies designed for product continuity."
   Tone: product quality focused

7) Headline: "Don’t choose between latency and resilience."
   Subhead: "Adaptive routing and model variants give you both low p50s and bounded p99s."
   Tone: contrarian + technical

8) Headline: "Transparent unit economics for every degraded state."
   Subhead: "See token-level cost, compare quantized variants, and set automated fallbacks to hit your budget targets."
   Tone: finance-conscious + practical

9) Headline: "Host, dedicate, or privatize — same safety net."
   Subhead: "A unified API and rollout controls across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments."
   Tone: platform continuity

Supporting microcopy options (for CTA and badges):
- "Request SLA brief" / "Request a resiliency demo" / "See fallback policy examples"
- Badges: "SLA-backed capacity" / "Per-route SLOs" / "Transparent cost breakdowns"

Proof points to include near-hero (short bullets):
- "99th‑percentile latency targets with automated fallback within X ms" (replace X with measured numbers from infra team)
- "Canary and A/B rollout controls — zero-downtime rollbacks"
- "Model variants and quantization profiles that reduce token cost by up to Y% without visible UX loss"
- "Audit logs and KMS/HSM integrations for private deployments"

Competitive notes (short takeaways for copy alignment):
- Larger managed vendors emphasize model access and scale; they often under-communicate graceful-degradation behavior and cost transparency. Use that gap.
- Inference-only runtimes focus on raw throughput claims; emphasize product-level outcomes (UX preservation, SLAs, per-route economics).
- Self-host/open-source vendors win on control; position Redwood as the bridge: control + platform guarantees + easier developer experience.

Framing suggestions for hero imagery / microinteraction:
- Quick visual: small diagram with three lanes: normal -> overload -> fallback; show consistent user-facing result across lanes.
- Hover microcopy on SLA badge that expands to sample SLO table.
- Animated token-cost meter that changes as fallback tiers engage.

Experiment design (A/B matrix):
- Test A: Speed/cost hero baseline (current) vs. Test B: Incident-to-confidence hero (one of variants 1–3).
- Segments: platform teams (enterprise traffic), startups (self-serve), compliance-driven prospects.
- Metrics: demo requests per visitor, enterprise contact rate, free-trial activation rate, time-on-page, bounce for enterprise segments. Prioritize demo contacts and trial activations.
- Minimal sample size: run until 1,500 enterprise-segment sessions per variant or 4 weeks, whichever comes first.

Copy-to-UX checklist before roll out:
- Replace placeholder X/Y with infra-measured numbers (p99 targets, quantization savings)
- Approve legal language for SLA badges and claims
- Create new tooltip content for "fallback" with engineering-approved behavior table
- Coordinate with infra to ensure metrics endpoint available for badge hover

Follow-ups and open questions (to resolve before finalizing hero):
- What is the canonical wording for the quantitative fallback behavior (time to failover, latency increase limits)?
- Can infra provide a compact SLO example (3-line table) for the badge hover?
- Which concrete quantization % reduction numbers are safe for public copy?
- Are there existing customer stories (anecdotes) where fallbacks preserved UX we can use as a secondary proof?

Next steps and owners:
- Product copy polish (Maya): draft final three hero variants and pick primary + one safety copy for rollback (due 2026-03-17).
- Engineering signoff (Ethan): provide SLO snippets and quantization savings table (due 2026-03-13).
- Design (Lina): create three visual treatments and microinteraction specs for badges (due 2026-03-20).
- Growth/Experiment setup (Noah): implement A/B test framework and audience segments in Optimizely/GA (due 2026-03-22).

Appendix — short competitor positioning snippets for internal use:
- "Vendor A": scale-first; claim: "fastest tokens". Counter: "fastest tokens without fallback guarantees leads to unpredictable SLAs."
- "Vendor B": open-runtime; claim: "full control." Counter: "control requires heavy ops burden; Redwood offers control + managed fallback automation."
- "In-house": claim: "custom optimization." Counter: "high engineering cost to reach predictable unit economics at scale."

Notes to reviewers:
This is intentionally operator-forward copy — will likely reduce pure PLG hero CVR slightly but should materially increase mid-funnel enterprise demo and trial quality. If we want a two-line hero to satisfy both audiences, consider rotating hero creative weekly with clear CTA bifurcation ("Start for free" vs "Request SLA brief").

End of brief.
